records.title: Record 2024 marine heat stress across the Western Indian Ocean, with more than 20 degree heating weeks for the first time
records.description: El Nino, a positive Indian Ocean Dipole and record global ocean temperatures built heat stress across the region from late 2023. CORDIO East Africa reported more than 8 degree heating weeks by February 2024 and over 12 by April, with pockets in Seychelles reaching 16. The 2026 GCRMN regional chapter states that 93% of the region's reefs passed 4 degree heating weeks in 2024-2025 and that values above 20 were documented for the first time.

location.name: Western Indian Ocean reef waters
location.detail: Heat stress mapped from the equator to about 20 S, strongest on the East African coast, the Seychelles and the Mascarenes; Mozambique Channel and southwest Madagascar saw less heat stress in 2024.

records.layer_rationale: A basin-scale thermal event driven by ENSO, the Indian Ocean Dipole and long-term warming.

notes.harm: CORDIO East Africa found about 80% of observed locations bleached and 40% with moderate to extreme mortality, and GCRMN reports more than 20 degree heating weeks for the first time (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: None of the cited sources documents a fishery closure or advisory tied to the heat stress itself; Down To Earth only flags tuna-route concern in 2026 (ref 4).
notes.scale: The heat stress spans the regional sea from the equator to about 20 S rather than a single reef (ref 1).
notes.duration: Record global temperatures from April 2023 and heat stress through 2024-2025 mean a year or more of exposure (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: A regional CORDIO report and the GCRMN Status of Coral Reefs 2025 chapter formally assess the event, but no emergency declaration is cited (refs 1, 3).

population_affected.note: The cited reports give reef and observation counts, not people affected.

key_measure.text: 93% of the region's reefs experienced more than 4 degree heating weeks in 2024-2025, and values exceeding 20 were documented in the region for the first time (GCRMN, 2026).

records.title: Rising seas and erosion breach sea walls and shrink Tanzania's Mafia, Unguja and Pemba coasts
records.description: Tanzania's environment minister told Parliament in April 2024 that sea level at Dar es Salaam has risen by an average of 6 mm a year since 2002, with erosion, loss of beaches and saltwater intrusion. The Citizen documented walls breached at Kilindoni on Mafia Island and a 2019 Zanzibar survey listing severely eroded sites on Unguja and Pemba. In September 2026 the Vice President told a UN General Assembly meeting that erosion, saltwater intrusion and flooding are growing risks, and a July 2026 review found coastal flood adaptation insufficient.

records.title: Kenya-Tanzania border flagged as an oil pollution hotspot as the Western Indian Ocean finalises a regional spill plan
records.description: A study by the Indian Ocean Commission, reported in July 2025, named the Kenya-Tanzania border near Mombasa and Dar es Salaam as one of seven hotspots for oil pollution from ships. Kenya ran a five-day response exercise in Mombasa on 7-11 July 2025, and in January 2026 experts from ten countries met in Zanzibar under the Nairobi Convention to finalise a Regional Contingency Plan.

location.type: Shipping lane and oil spill risk area
location.detail: Waters between Mombasa and Dar es Salaam; response exercise held at Bandari Maritime Academy and Nyali Beach, Mombasa.

records.layer_rationale: Shipping-related oil spill risk and the regional response framework.

notes.harm: No spill is documented; the Indian Ocean Commission study flags the border as one of seven ship oil-pollution hotspots, a potential harm (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or advisory results from the finding (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: The risk and the regional plan span the Western Indian Ocean's ten Nairobi Convention countries (ref 3).
notes.duration: The cited items run from July 2025 to January 2026, several months of work on the plan (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: The Nairobi Convention press release on a meeting to finalise the Regional Contingency Plan is a formal treaty process step (ref 3).

population_affected.note: Not applicable to a risk assessment in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: The Kenya-Tanzania border is one of seven oil pollution hotspots for ships in the region's Indian Ocean waters, per an Indian Ocean Commission study (The Standard, 10 July 2025).

measures.note: Nairobi Convention press release (ref 3).

trend.note: Preparedness steps are documented; no spill is recorded in the cited sources.

records.title: Severe 2024 mass coral bleaching across the Western Indian Ocean erases two decades of hard coral gain
records.description: CORDIO East Africa's regional report found that 2024 heat stress, driven by El Nino and a positive Indian Ocean Dipole, caused widespread bleaching and mortality on reefs from Kenya and Tanzania to Seychelles, Mauritius, Madagascar and the Comoros. The 2025 GCRMN regional chapter models regional hard coral cover falling from 33.9% in 2023 to 25.9% in 2024, comparable to 1999 levels, and reports 66% cumulative coral mortality at Mayotte after the bleaching and Cyclone Chido.

location.name: Western Indian Ocean coral reefs
location.detail: Reefs from the Kenyan and Tanzanian coast to Seychelles, the Mascarenes, Madagascar, the Comoros and Mayotte; bleaching reported between the equator and 20 degrees S

records.layer_rationale: Heat stress killed and bleached reef-building corals, a loss of marine habitat.
secondary_drivers: El Nino and positive Indian Ocean Dipole

notes.harm: CORDIO's 238 observations (to end June 2024) put high and extreme mortality at 10.6% of sites and medium to extreme mortality at about 40% (ref 1); the GCRMN chapter models hard coral cover down from 33.9% in 2023 to 25.9% in 2024 (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited sources describe reef dependence of coastal communities (ref 2) but report no fishery or tourism closure tied to the 2024 bleaching, so no disruption is scored.
notes.scale: Bleaching was reported from eight countries and heat stress above 12 Degree Heating Weeks spanned the equator to 20 degrees S (ref 1), a regional-sea scale.
notes.duration: The GCRMN chapter calls 2024 to 2025 the most severe regional heat stress event and states 93% of reefs exceeded 4 DHW, with recovery outlook uncertain (ref 2).
notes.significance: A regional bleaching report by the GCRMN regional coordinator (ref 1) and the 2025 GCRMN chapter (ref 2) are formal assessments, but no enforcement or legal action applies.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: CORDIO East Africa: about 80% of observed locations bleached, 40% with medium to extreme mortality; GCRMN: regional hard coral cover fell from 33.9% (2023) to 25.9% (2024).

trend.note: Heat stress built from January 2024 and the GCRMN chapter calls 2024 to 2025 the most severe event on record for the region (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Chagos treaty ratification stalls as the future of the 640,000 km2 marine protected area stays undecided
records.description: The UK and Mauritius signed a treaty on 22 May 2025 recognising Mauritian sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago, with Mauritius committed to create its own marine protected area and the UK support terms left to a separate instrument. In April 2026 a Loughborough University legal expert reported the UK had shelved the implementing legislation after the US withdrew support, and Mauritius said it was exploring legal avenues.

location.name: Chagos Archipelago and its marine protected area
location.type: Marine protected area and treaty process
location.detail: British Indian Ocean Territory (Chagos Archipelago), central Indian Ocean, including the 640,000 km2 UK-declared no-take MPA

records.layer_rationale: A sovereignty treaty process decides who governs and protects one of the largest no-take marine protected areas.

notes.harm: Mongabay describes the MPA's reefs as among the healthiest in the world, with nearly 300 reef-building coral species, and the cited sources document no ecological harm from the treaty process (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The MPA is a no-take reserve that Chagossians criticise as a pretext to keep them out, and Bernadette Dugasse said she was not consulted (ref 1).
notes.scale: The MPA covers about 640,000 km2 of ocean, a national-waters scale (ref 1).
notes.duration: The MPA dates from 2010 and the treaty was signed on 22 May 2025 but ratification was still unresolved in April 2026 (refs 1, 5).
notes.significance: A signed UK-Mauritius treaty on 22 May 2025 (ref 1), written answers in the UK House of Commons on MPA support (refs 2, 3) and a shelved ratification bill (ref 5) are treaty-level actions.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: IOTC adopts yellowfin catch limits for 2027 to 2028 while the 2024 stock assessment stays contested
records.description: At its 30th session in the Maldives in May 2026 the Indian Ocean Tuna Commission adopted Resolution 26/01 on interim catch limits for yellowfin tuna, reported by industry body Europeche as a 436,867 tonne total allowable catch for 2027 and 2028 against current catches of 489,742 tonnes. The 2024 assessment found the stock not overfished with an 86% probability of Kobe Green, but the Commission recorded important data uncertainties, and an NGO submission says objecting fleets, notably Oman, expanded catches sharply.

location.name: Indian Ocean yellowfin tuna fishery (IOTC area)
location.type: Tuna stock and regional fisheries management area
location.detail: Indian Ocean high seas and coastal-state waters from Somalia and Oman to Mozambique, Madagascar, Seychelles and the Mascarenes

records.layer_rationale: The finding concerns the exploitation and management of a commercially fished tuna stock.

notes.harm: The 2024 assessment found yellowfin not overfished (86% probability of Kobe Green) but the Commission recorded important data uncertainties, and an earlier overfished declaration dates from 2015 (refs 1, 5).
notes.livelihoods: Resolution 26/01 sets catch limits and quotas that constrain fleets, and a Galmudug State fisheries minister estimated USD 300 million a year is lost to IUU fishing in Somalia (refs 2, 3, 4).
notes.scale: The IOTC area of competence is the whole Indian Ocean basin and the stock is fished by over two dozen members (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Yellowfin was declared overfished in 2015 and interim plans have run since then, with the Commission deferring yellowfin proposals in 2024 and 2025 (refs 1, 2, 5).
notes.significance: Resolution 26/01 was adopted by the Commission on 11 to 15 May 2026 and binds members from 19 September 2026 unless objections are lodged (ref 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Four vessels hijacked off Somalia in April and May 2026 as the IMB reports a persistent piracy threat
records.description: The ICC International Maritime Bureau's mid-year report for January to June 2026 recorded four hijackings in the Somali region between April and May 2026, plus further attacks and suspicious approaches in June. The IMB attributes 94% of crew taken hostage worldwide in the period to Somali pirates and says they often operate from hijacked fishing vessels or dhows used as mother ships.

location.name: Somali coast and western Indian Ocean shipping lanes
location.detail: Waters off the Somali coast, the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean; the sources give no precise positions for the 2026 hijackings

records.layer_rationale: Piracy is a security and governance risk to commercial shipping and fishing vessels, not a pollutant or habitat issue.
secondary_drivers: Hijacked fishing vessels and dhows used as mother ships

notes.harm: The IMB recorded 67 crew taken hostage worldwide in January to June 2026 and attributes 94% of hostages to Somali pirates (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The IMB urged ships transiting the Somali coast and Gulf of Aden to keep strict anti-piracy watches and follow Best Management Practices (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The four hijackings and further attacks span the Somali coast, the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean, a regional sea (ref 2).
notes.duration: The IMB says Somali piracy remains a persistent threat and that vessels were previously targeted more than 1,000 nautical miles from the Somali coast (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The IMB, as the ICC's reporting centre, issued a formal mid-year advisory on 9 July 2026 asking for continued naval presence (ref 1).

records.title: Mozambique LNG restarts at Afungi while resettled fishing villages remain about 10 km from the sea
records.description: TotalEnergies and Mozambique announced the full restart of the USD 20 billion Mozambique LNG project at Afungi on 29 January 2026 after a force majeure that began in 2021, with first LNG targeted for 2029. Mongabay reports that NGOs and affected communities say several fishing villages were resettled about 10 km inland, far from traditional fishing grounds, with insufficient mitigation, and Reuters describes the site as an enclave reachable only by sea or air.

location.name: Afungi LNG site, Palma, Cabo Delgado
location.type: LNG plant and coastal resettlement area
location.detail: Afungi Peninsula near Palma, Cabo Delgado Province, northern Mozambique, on the Mozambique Channel and Rovuma basin coast

records.layer_rationale: An offshore-gas LNG development shapes coastal fishing access, resettlement and local economies.

notes.harm: Friends of the Earth alleges killings and communities fleeing, and TotalEnergies rejects all accusations, while Justiça Ambiental warns of environmental risks in an ecologically sensitive area (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Several fishing villages were resettled about 10 km inland, far from traditional fishing grounds, with NGOs and communities saying livelihoods were harmed and mitigation insufficient (ref 2).
notes.scale: The documented resettlement and containment concern one coastal site at Afungi and Palma (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Force majeure ran from 2021 to the lifting announced in late 2025, with the full restart on 29 January 2026 and first LNG targeted for 2029 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Two legal proceedings against TotalEnergies are under way in France, including a manslaughter investigation, and the UK withdrew USD 1.15 billion in export finance (ref 1).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

records.title: Dar es Salaam port congestion eases under DP World concession while sovereignty concerns persist
records.description: Tanzania Ports Authority signed a 30-year concession for DP World to operate Dar es Salaam port in October 2023, and DP World took over operations on 15 April 2024. Tanzania's government told Parliament average vessel waiting time fell from 46 days in May 2024 to 7 days in September 2024, while opposition politicians, activists and clerics criticised the deal as a threat to sovereignty and security.

notes.harm: The cited pages document no pollution, dredging or habitat effect at the port, and neither mentions environmental impact (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Vessel waiting time averaged 46 days in May 2024 before falling to 7 days in September 2024, a shipping delay that affected cargo flows (ref 2).
notes.scale: The congestion and concession concern a single port (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The delays are documented over May to September 2024 and the concession runs 30 years from October 2023 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The concession is a signed agreement with the Tanzania Ports Authority and the throughput figures were given in a Parliament statement on 1 November 2024 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Zanzibar seaweed farmers report heat-driven losses as yields fall and women turn to sponge farming
records.description: Zanzibar has nearly 25,000 seaweed farmers, about 90% of them women, and the Citizen reported in August 2024 that seaweed production fell 47% between 2002 and 2021. A peer-reviewed survey of 183 farmers in Micheweni, Pemba, found average household yields fell from 4,480 kg in 2016 to 2,422 kg in 2020, attributed to heat stress and winds, and AFP reported in November 2025 that some farmers are switching to sponge cultivation.

notes.harm: Farmers say hot temperatures have killed or rotted seaweed, and an AFP report quotes project manager Ali Mahmudi that 'hot temperatures have killed seaweed' (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: Seaweed is Zanzibar's third-largest income source for nearly 25,000 farmers, and Micheweni household yields fell from 4,480 kg to 2,422 kg between 2016 and 2020 (refs 1, 3).
notes.scale: The 47% production decline is reported for Zanzibar as a whole while the yield survey covers two shehias in Pemba (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: The Citizen cites a 47% fall between 2002 and 2021, and the declines are still being reported in 2025 (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: The evidence is a peer-reviewed survey and news reports with no notice, order or listing by an authority (refs 1, 2, 3).

records.title: Distant-water fleet fishes the Saya de Malha Bank with little tracking as protection calls continue
records.description: The Outlaw Ocean Project reported in March 2025 that more than 200 distant-water vessels, mostly from Sri Lanka and Taiwan, have gathered along the deeper edge of the Saya de Malha Bank between Mauritius and Seychelles, and that virtually no one tracks or polices them. The bank, about 40,000 km2, is described in the reporting as one of the world's largest seagrass meadows and a candidate for protection, while the extent of seagrass there is not settled in the sources opened.

location.name: Saya de Malha Bank, Mascarene Plateau
location.detail: Submerged bank on the Mascarene Plateau between Mauritius and Seychelles, largely beyond national jurisdiction

records.layer_rationale: Largely unregulated high-seas fishing pressure on an offshore bank and its seabed habitat.
secondary_drivers: Weak monitoring on the high seas

notes.harm: The Outlaw Ocean Project says the area is being decimated by a multinational fleet, an assertion not backed by a catch or habitat survey in the pages opened (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Record 2024-25 marine heatwave along more than 1,500 km of Western Australia's coast
records.description: The WA Coral Bleaching Group, convened by the Australian Institute of Marine Science, reported that the 2024/25 marine heatwave was the longest, largest and most intense on record for Western Australia. Surface temperatures reached up to 4 degrees C above average and heat stress peaked in December 2024 to January 2025 and again in March to April 2025 before receding in May. Heat stress reached 20 degree heating weeks at central Ningaloo and up to 30 at some Pilbara reefs, with bleaching and mortality following; coral outcomes are covered separately.

location.name: Northwest and west coast of WA (Kimberley to Ningaloo)
location.detail: Western Australia, from the Kimberley and Rowley Shoals south through the Pilbara to Ningaloo; heat spread along more than 1,500 km of coastline (ref 1).

records.layer_rationale: A prolonged thermal anomaly in coastal waters, with the physical heat event itself as the primary issue.
secondary_drivers: Absence of monsoonal storms and cyclones

notes.harm: Surveys found coral bleaching and death from medium (11-30%) to extreme (over 90%) across systems up to 1,500 km apart, including 61-90% death at Rowley Shoals' Mermaid and Clerke Reefs in April 2025 (ref 1, ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited sources describe no closure, restriction or advisory tied to the heatwave itself, so no livelihood disruption is scored.
notes.scale: Heat affected seas along more than 1,500 km of the Western Australian coast, a national coastline rather than a single site (ref 1).
notes.duration: AIMS partners began monitoring in September 2024 and temperatures only began to recede in May 2025, roughly eight months of heat stress (ref 2).
notes.significance: Scientists and managers of the WA Coral Bleaching Group formally described it as the longest, largest and most intense on record for the state, but no enforcement or emergency declaration is cited (ref 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Heat stress reached 20 degree heating weeks at central Ningaloo and a maximum of 30 at central Pilbara reefs; 4 DHW is where bleaching is likely (AIMS scientist, The Conversation, 12 Aug 2025).

records.title: Prolonged Karenia algal bloom kills marine life along South Australia's gulf and island coasts
records.description: A harmful algal bloom dominated by Karenia species was first detected off the Fleurieu Peninsula in March 2025 during a marine heatwave and had spread across Gulf St Vincent, Kangaroo Island, Yorke Peninsula and parts of Spencer Gulf. The SARDI chief said it affected about 30 per cent of the state's coastline; it caused mass deaths of marine life, foam on Adelaide beaches, respiratory irritation and fishing and tourism losses. A government report released in July 2026 concluded that floodwater nutrients, a coastal upwelling and the marine heatwave together created the conditions, and by February 2026 the main activity had moved to south-western Yorke Peninsula.

location.name: Gulf St Vincent, Fleurieu, Yorke and Kangaroo Island coasts
location.detail: South Australia; Gulf St Vincent, Fleurieu Peninsula, Kangaroo Island, Yorke Peninsula and parts of Spencer Gulf and the Eyre Peninsula coast.

records.layer_rationale: A nutrient-fuelled harmful algal bloom in coastal waters, with nutrient input, upwelling and marine heat as drivers.

notes.harm: AAP reported hundreds of reports of marine deaths including sharks, penguins, flathead, squid, crabs and rock lobsters, and OzFish counted more than 200 species killed (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Commercial fishing catches dwindled (ref 2) and the SA government has restricted commercial scalefish and blue crab fishing in the Gulf St Vincent and Kangaroo Island zone from 1 November 2025 and committed 48 million dollars to coastal communities and businesses (ref 3, ref 6).
notes.scale: SARDI's chief estimated the bloom affected about 30 per cent of the state's coastline, roughly 1,500 km, across two gulfs and several peninsulas (ref 2).
notes.duration: First detected in March 2025, still present in January 2026 with a hotspot on south-western Yorke Peninsula, and described as lasting over 12 months by July 2026 (refs 3, 5).
notes.significance: SA Health issued advice for people with asthma, the state and federal governments funded response packages and the SA government released a SARDI peer-reviewed drivers report in July 2026, but no emergency declaration is cited (refs 4, 6).

records.title: Sri Lanka's Supreme Court orders US$1 billion for the X-Press Pearl disaster; first payment not made
records.description: The container ship X-Press Pearl burned and sank off Colombo in 2021, releasing an estimated 70 to 75 billion plastic nurdles plus chemicals and bunker oil along Sri Lanka's west coast. On 24 July 2025 the Supreme Court held the owner, operator and local agent jointly liable and ordered an initial US$1 billion in compensation in instalments within a year. X-Press Feeders said it was unable to pay the first US$250 million due on 23 September 2025, and the local agent told the court it lacked the resources.

notes.livelihoods: A year-long fishing ban hit the affected coastline and the Diplomat estimated about 20,000 Negombo-area families abandoned fishing (refs 3, 5).
notes.scale: Initial contamination covered an 80 km stretch of the west coast, later spreading across about 750 km, a national coastline (ref 5).
notes.duration: The 2021 spill is still producing contamination and litigation in 2026; beach cleaning in Negombo was continuing four years later (ref 5).
notes.significance: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka judgment of 24 July 2025 in SC/FR 168/2021 and connected cases ordered US$1 billion, a compensation commission and further investigations (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Maldives reclamation boom: over 4,000 hectares of new land raises reef and flooding concerns
records.description: A peer-reviewed study published in May 2026 mapped 109 community land reclamation projects on inhabited Maldivian islands between 2000 and 2024, adding at least 4,198 hectares, with a peak of 25 projects started in 2023. Reclamation is promoted as protection against sea-level rise, but the study and earlier reporting say it disrupts reef systems and sediment flows and can raise wave energy, erosion and flood exposure. Human Rights Watch, quoted in 2023, said projects were often rushed and cited buried mangroves and damaged reefs at Addu.

location.detail: Maldives; 109 projects on inhabited islands, 71% of reclaimed land in the Central Region and over half in Kaafu Atoll, including Hulhumalé (ref 1). Coordinates are Hulhumalé.

records.layer_rationale: Coastal adaptation to sea-level rise that may itself raise flooding and erosion risk.

notes.harm: Human Rights Watch, quoted by AFP, said 70 per cent of mangroves on Kulhudhuffushi were buried by an airport reclamation and a project at Addu damaged coral reefs (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The same AFP report said the Addu reclamation damaged coral reefs that fishermen depended on, and local critics say the new land has not met economic needs (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: Projects span the national archipelago, with 109 projects across inhabited islands and 4,198 hectares reclaimed (ref 1).
notes.duration: Reclamation has been continuous since 2000 and 19 projects were still ongoing when the study was compiled (ref 1).
notes.significance: Human Rights Watch published a formal report criticising unenforced environmental rules, and a peer-reviewed national assessment followed, but no enforcement action is cited (refs 1, 2).

The department said it would spend Rs 303.5 million on protective structures in 2025.

records.title: Plastic debris keeps washing onto Cocos (Keeling) Islands beaches
records.description: A 2019 study estimated 414 million plastic items weighing 238 tonnes on the Cocos (Keeling) Islands. Sea Shepherd Australia's 2024 clean-up, its fifth consecutive year, removed 9.3 tonnes from about 10 km of coastline on five islands, including more than 700,000 pieces of lightweight plastic and 2.7 tonnes of ghost gear. Sea Shepherd said the islands burn waste openly because of biosecurity rules and shipping costs.

notes.harm: The 2019 survey estimated 414 million items and 238 tonnes of plastic with about 93% buried to 10 cm, and Sea Shepherd found hermit crabs using plastic lids as shells and wildlife trapped in containers (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited sources report no beach closure or fishery disruption; tourism is the islands' main income source but no loss is documented (ref 2).
notes.scale: The pollution is concentrated on a small island group, scored as a single site rather than a regional sea (ref 2).
notes.duration: Sea Shepherd has returned five consecutive years since 2020 and removed over 49 tonnes, showing chronic recurrence (ref 1).

records.title: Plastic pellets found on all nine surveyed Sri Lankan west-coast beaches in 2025
records.description: A survey of nine west-coast beaches over 13 weeks from July to September 2025, presented in June 2026, found nurdles at every site, from about 15 to more than 3,000 per standardised search. records.title: Record marine heatwave bleaches and kills corals along 1,500 km of Western Australia's reefs, including Ningaloo and the Rowley Shoals
records.description: The Western Australian Government's conservation department (DBCA) and the Australian Institute of Marine Science (AIMS) report high levels of coral bleaching and mortality across the north-west atolls, Kimberley, Pilbara and northern Gascoyne coasts after a marine heatwave that began around December 2024. AIMS describes it as the longest, largest and most intense marine heatwave on record for the state, and DBCA says follow-up surveys continue through 2025 and into 2026 to establish the full impact.

location.name: WA north-west reefs: Ningaloo to the Kimberley
location.detail: Western Australia: Ningaloo Marine Park, Exmouth Gulf, Montebello and Barrow Islands, Dampier Archipelago, Rowley Shoals, Kimberley coast

records.layer_rationale: Habitat loss on reefs driven by prolonged marine heatwave heat stress.

notes.harm: DBCA reported a 60 per cent decline in coral cover at long-term sites in the Montebello and Barrow Islands reserves and very high mortality at shallow Dampier Archipelago sites (ref 1); AIMS-reported mortality of 61-90 per cent at the Rowley Shoals monitored sites (refs 3, 4).
notes.livelihoods: No closure or restriction is documented in the cited pages; a Exmouth glass-bottom boat operator said the loss of about 90 per cent of coral in some patches had potential to affect his business (ref 3), so this is scored 0 pending evidence of an actual restriction.
notes.scale: Bleaching and mortality were reported along a 1,500 km stretch of the WA coast (refs 3, 4), a national coastline rather than a single reef.
notes.duration: Heat stress ran from about December 2024 (ref 2) and DBCA still described high bleaching and mortality almost 12 months later, with surveys planned through 2026 (ref 1); AIMS estimated reefs may need 10-15 years to recover (ref 4).
notes.significance: DBCA and AIMS published formal monitoring findings and the AIMS-led WA Coral Bleaching Group documented the event as the worst on record for the state (refs 1, 3); no enforcement or treaty action applies.

records.title: Maldives suspends coastal dredging during 2024 coral bleaching; central atoll reefs show uneven recovery in 2025 survey
records.description: The Maldives Marine Research Institute reported localised bleaching in March 2024 and the Environmental Protection Agency suspended major coastal development, such as dredging and reclamation, over the bleaching window. A Reef Check partner report on October 2025 surveys in Ari, South Male and Vaavu atolls says the archipelago escaped a mass bleaching event in 2025 after severe thermal stress in 2024 but shows uneven recovery, with inner lagoon reefs recovering more slowly than outer slopes.

location.name: Central Maldives atolls (Ari, South Male, Vaavu)
location.detail: Republic of Maldives, central atolls of the Laccadive Sea and northern Indian Ocean

records.layer_rationale: Thermal-stress damage and slow recovery of reef habitat, compounded by coastal dredging.

notes.harm: The Biosphere Expeditions report on October 2025 surveys describes stunted recovery on inner lagoonal reefs after the 2024 thermal stress (ref 3); no mortality percentage was opened, so harm is scored as limited.
notes.livelihoods: The EPA ordered a temporary halt to dredging, reclamation, beach nourishment, sand pumping and cable laying on reefs during the bleaching window (ref 1), a restriction on coastal developers.
notes.scale: The EPA order applied to all major coastal development nationwide and the survey covers three central atolls (refs 1, 3).
notes.duration: Localised bleaching was reported from 17 March 2024 (ref 2) and the October 2025 survey still found uneven recovery (ref 3), spanning more than a year.
notes.significance: The EPA issued a formal order suspending activity under EIA and dredging permits (ref 1); a related headline on the same page reports the measures were later lifted.

records.title: Woodside's Browse gas development near Scott Reef remains in WA and federal environmental assessment after the 2025 amended proposal
records.description: Woodside Energy's proposed Browse development would drill for gas in the Torosa reservoir, about 425 km north of Broome, around Scott Reef. The WA Environmental Protection Authority has assessed the state-waters component since 2019, accepted an amended proposal in August 2025 after more than 17,700 submissions, and has yet to publish its recommendation in the sources reviewed. Conservation groups say the plans still risk spills, seismic noise and harm to pygmy blue whales and green turtles; Woodside says it continues to work with regulators.

records.title: Western Australia closes West Coast demersal fishing to commercial fishers and bans recreational boat fishing for dhufish and snapper to 2027
records.description: After stock assessments showed several demersal species including WA dhufish under severe threat, the State Government announced in December 2025 that the West Coast bioregion (Kalbarri to Augusta) will not reopen to boat-based recreational demersal fishing until spring 2027 and is permanently closed to commercial demersal fishing from 1 January 2026, with a licence buyback. Other regions get catch reductions and new limits under a $29.2 million package.

notes.duration: The boat-based recreational closure runs 21 months to a September 2027 reopening and the commercial closure is permanent (refs 1, 2); recovery is described as decades-long (ref 3).

records.title: South Australian gulf fisheries stay closed to commercial fishing into 2027 after the harmful algal bloom

Industry says more than 100 marine scalefish fishers could not fish by April 2026 and that recovery could take five to ten years or more; a recreational king George whiting closure was lifted early in July 2026 as spawning had largely occurred.

records.title: Australian sea lion remains in decline at key colonies in South Australia and Western Australia despite gillnet closures
records.description: A 2026 conference abstract by South Australian Research and Development Institute scientists says the endangered Australian sea lion has declined by more than 60 per cent over four decades; bycatch-reduction measures have produced partial recoveries at some sites, but several colonies including two of the largest continue to decline. The abstract points to nutritional stress, the algal bloom and a risk from avian influenza. In Western Australia the EPA recommended sea lion haul-out protections for the Port of Geraldton upgrade.

records.title: Sewage-derived debris balls wash up on Sydney, South Coast and Central Coast beaches from October 2024
records.description: Black and grey debris balls, mostly marble-sized, washed up on Sydney's Eastern Suburbs beaches from October 2024, then on the South Coast, the Northern Beaches (January 2025) and Central Coast beaches (August 2025). NSW EPA analysis found hair, waste cooking oil, faecal material and hydrocarbons, and in April 2025 named Sydney Water's land-based sewage system as the most likely source, narrowing it to the Malabar system in October 2025. The EPA issued Sydney Water a Preliminary Investigation Notice; the EPA page lists no confirmed reports since August 2025.

records.title: Deep oxygen falls below guideline range in Macquarie Harbour, home of the endangered Maugean skate
records.description: The Tasmanian EPA reports that dissolved oxygen in Macquarie Harbour held steady in the top 15 to 20 metres between July 2025 and June 2026 but declined below that, falling under the interim guideline range in the central and south-east segments. The decline coincided with the wettest spring and summer since 1998 and weaker ocean recharge, and the regulator required the three salmon producers to offset 10.3 tonnes of oxygen demand a day. The harbour is the only place the Maugean skate, listed Endangered since 2004, is now found.

records.title: Total nitrogen exceeds guideline values across Storm Bay as salmon farming expands under a staged nitrogen limit
records.description: Storm Bay's 2023/24 broadscale monitoring report (May 2023 to April 2024) found total nitrogen above default guideline values at multiple sites over multiple months in one region, continuing a high-nitrogen trend recorded since 2021. The report, prepared for Tassal and Huon Aquaculture, attributes the pattern to a regional signal such as shifting boundary currents or river inputs, with no clear link to distance from the leases, and found no broad-scale change in sediments or seabed animals. The EPA set a Stage 1 Total Permissible Dissolved Nitrogen Output of 1,747 tonnes for the Storm Bay Regional Area from 1 January 2025.

records.description: The Derwent Estuary Program's State of Timtumili Minanya/Derwent 2025 report summarises Hobart's estuary as under pressure from elevated nutrients, localised algal growth, seasonal low dissolved oxygen in the upper estuary, and legacy metal contamination. Sewage plants supply most of the dissolved inorganic nitrogen and total phosphorus, and total nitrogen rose in the upper estuary. A TasWater plant closure and upgrade is expected to cut nutrient loads by up to 58% for nitrogen and 42% for phosphorus.

records.title: Reef nutrient enrichment near Long Bay salmon farm keeps a 48-tonne nitrogen limit in place at Port Arthur
records.description: IMAS surveys commissioned by the Tasmanian EPA showed the effects of significant nutrient enrichment on rocky reefs 100 m and 400 m from the Tassal salmon farm in Long Bay, Port Arthur. On 1 September 2026 the EPA kept the Total Permissible Dissolved Nitrogen Output for the lease at 48 tonnes until 31 July 2027, saying algae levels showed no significant change in 2024 and 2025 and that water quality across the wider Port Arthur area had not declined. It renewed the licence to 30 November 2027 and ordered further science on nutrient movement.

records.title: Moa Point wastewater plant failure sends untreated sewage into Cook Strait off Wellington's south coast
records.description: Flooding on 4 February 2026 knocked out power and treatment at the Moa Point Wastewater Treatment Plant, and untreated wastewater has since discharged into Tarakena Bay and out the long outfall into Cook Strait. Tarakena Bay is a no-go area and people are told not to collect or eat kaimoana from Ōwhiro Bay to Breaker Bay. Tiaki Wai says the Crown Review found no single point of failure, Greater Wellington Regional Council has filed court charges (announced 1 October 2026), and the plant is due to resume treatment in November 2026 with full operations expected by February 2027.

records.title: Hauraki Gulf report finds 1,793 dry-weather sewage overflows in a year and sediment above guideline rates
records.description: The Hauraki Gulf Forum's State of our Gulf 2026 report rates the Gulf as under pressure, recording 1,793 uncontrolled dry-weather wastewater overflow events across 19 Auckland catchments in 2024/25. More than a third of monitored intertidal sites accumulate sediment above guideline rates, and nutrient enrichment, microalgal blooms and reduced dissolved oxygen are becoming more evident in parts of the Gulf. Network separation and Watercare's Central Interceptor, planned for mid-2026, aim to cut wet-weather overflows to the Waitemata Harbour.

records.title: Marine heatwaves reach Tasmania, Bass Strait and the NSW coast in summer 2024-25, with a salmon die-off and a NSW fish kill
records.description: A peer-reviewed review of the 2024/25 season reports localised marine heatwaves off south-east Tasmania from late November 2024, covering most of the state by March 2025 and reaching southern Victoria and Bass Strait by late March. Impacts included salp, Noctiluca and moon jellyfish blooms, reduced little penguin returns, and a salmon bacterial disease outbreak causing mass mortality of farmed Atlantic salmon in southern Tasmania. Off the NSW south coast, short moderate-to-strong heatwaves preceded a mid-March fish kill of thousands of threadfin leatherjacket after temperatures dropped 4 to 6 C in 48 hours.

notes.livelihoods: A rickettsia outbreak linked to warm water caused mass mortality of farmed Atlantic salmon in southern Tasmania, and an abalone mortality at an NSW processing facility was attributed to heat-stressed stock or handling (ref 1).
notes.scale: The heatwaves covered most of Tasmania, Bass Strait, southern Victoria and the NSW south coast (ref 1).
notes.duration: Localised heatwaves began in late November 2024 and extended to most of Tasmania by March 2025, while NSW events lasted under 20 days each (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Tasmanian Government issued a marine heatwave information sheet and a response plan, and researchers ran national marine climate briefings advertised by the Fisheries Research and Development Corporation (refs 1, 2).

records.title: New Zealand waters warming 0.2 to 0.3 C a decade, fastest off the east coast and in the Tasman Sea
records.description: An Earth Sciences New Zealand report for Fisheries New Zealand, released in October 2025, finds average sea surface temperatures around New Zealand warmed 0.2 to 0.3 C per decade from 1982 to 2022, with trends especially pronounced off eastern New Zealand, in the Tasman Sea and over the Chatham Rise. Some recent marine heatwaves have already exceeded historic baselines by 5 C and could exceed them by 10 C by 2100 under high emissions. The 2026 State of our Gulf report links Hauraki Gulf heatwaves to temporary kelp loss and seabird breeding stress.

records.title: New Zealand coastal flood losses to infrastructure projected to nearly double by 2075
records.description: A study by Earth Sciences New Zealand for Te Waihanga, the New Zealand Infrastructure Commission, projects that under a high-emissions scenario coastal flooding losses to infrastructure grow from about $165 million a year in 2025 to $325 million in 2075. Hawke's Bay faces the largest increase relative to its network size, rising from $43 million to about $89 million a year across inland and coastal flooding. The commission says sea levels are rising and communities and networks designed for yesterday's conditions face greater pressure.

location.name: New Zealand coastline
location.detail: New Zealand's coastline, with Hawke's Bay, West Coast, Nelson-Tasman, Manawatu-Whanganui and Bay of Plenty showing the highest relative increases in flood losses.

records.layer_rationale: Rising sea levels increase the frequency and cost of coastal flooding, a physical coastal hazard.

notes.harm: Coastal flooding losses to infrastructure are modelled at $165 million a year in 2025 and $325 million in 2075, as book-value losses rather than replacement cost (ref 1); these are projected, not recorded, damages.
notes.livelihoods: The study models losses to infrastructure and private buildings and documents no coastal flood closure or displacement (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The assessment covers every New Zealand region, so it concerns the national coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: The projection runs from 2025 to 2075, with coastal losses growing gradually but at an accelerating rate (ref 2).
notes.significance: A formal commissioned report from Te Waihanga, published 9 July 2026 to support a National Infrastructure Plan priority (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Coastal flooding losses to New Zealand infrastructure are expected to grow from $165 million per year in 2025 to $325 million in 2075 under the SSP3-7.0 high-emissions scenario (Te Waihanga, July 2026).

records.title: Ex-Tropical Cyclone Alfred causes severe coastal erosion on the northern New South Wales coast in March 2025
records.description: Between 3 and 14 March 2025, Alfred brought strong winds, heavy rain, flooding and coastal erosion to northern New South Wales including the Northern Rivers, with gusts over 120 km/h recorded at Byron Bay. The Australian Institute for Disaster Resilience reports major coastal erosion in northern NSW and southern Queensland, with sand scarps up to about 6 metres high on some beaches, and the NSW Reconstruction Authority describes severe coastal erosion in northern NSW. The Queensland side of the event is filed separately.

notes.duration: Alfred affected northern NSW between 3 and 14 March 2025, a storm event of about two weeks (ref 1).
notes.significance: AIDR included the event in its Major Incidents Report 2024-25, and the NSW Reconstruction Authority lists it as a recent regional risk event (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Taranaki seabed iron-sand mining bid declined in draft by the Fast-track panel, then withdrawn in 2026
records.description: Trans-Tasman Resources applied under the Fast-track Approvals Act to extract up to 50 million tonnes of seabed sediment a year in the South Taranaki Bight. In February 2026 the expert panel issued a draft decision to decline, citing credible risk of harm to Maui dolphins, kororā (little penguins) and fairy prions, and the company then withdrew its application. Opponents say the withdrawal leaves open a possible new application, and the company said the panel misunderstood key foundations of its case.

notes.livelihoods: No fishery closure or lost income is reported in the cited sources; the panel cut the applicant's job estimates, which concern the project's benefits (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: The proposed licence area is a single seabed block 22 to 36 km off Patea, expanded from 66 km2 to 243 km2 in 2024 per Greenpeace (ref 4).
notes.duration: The dispute has run since a 2014 EPA refusal through the 2021 Supreme Court ruling to the 2026 Fast-track process, over a decade of proceedings (ref 4).
notes.significance: A Fast-track expert panel issued a draft decision to decline in February 2026, and the Supreme Court dismissed the company's earlier appeal in 2021 (refs 1, 3, 4).

records.title: Maugean skate in Macquarie Harbour: salmon-farm oxygen concerns and a 2025 change to federal approval powers
records.description: The endangered Maugean skate lives only in Macquarie Harbour on Tasmania's west coast, where salmon farms operate. A 2023 University of Tasmania study cited in news reports found its population rapidly halved between 2014 and 2021, and amendments passed in 2025 limit the federal minister's power to revisit past salmon-farming approvals. Environmental groups and some MPs are calling for intervention, while the industry and local officials welcomed the amendments.

notes.duration: The decline spans 2014 to 2021, a federal review since November 2023 and 2025 dissolved-oxygen declines reported by EPA Tasmania (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Parliament passed EPBC Act amendments in 2025 limiting the minister's power to revoke salmon approvals, and an EPBC review began in November 2023 (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Tasmanian salmon farms lose about 20,000 tonnes of fish to mortality in 2025
records.description: Atlantic salmon mortality data published by the Tasmanian EPA show at least four million fish died prematurely at Tasmanian farms in 2025, a total of 20,133 tonnes, with losses rising in the last three months of the year. Earlier government data obtained by a campaign group showed about 1,100 tonnes died in Macquarie Harbour between September 2023 and March 2024. The industry body says mortality is part of normal production. An unprecedented salmon mortality event ran from February to early May 2025 in the lower D'Entrecasteaux Channel, where Huon Aquaculture and Tassal farm. Congealed fish oil from dead salmon washed up at Verona Sands, Randalls Bay, Roaring Bay, Drip Beach and western South Bruny Island beaches, which the EPA treats as a loss of containment of a controlled waste. Over 5,500 tonnes of salmon mortality waste was received in February, some oil globules held oxytetracycline residues, and the EPA directed both companies on 6 March 2025 to remove dead fish.

location.name: Tasmanian salmon farms (statewide)
location.detail: Tasmania, Australia; the cited pieces refer to farms statewide and to Macquarie Harbour, without naming farm sites for the 2025 totals.

records.layer_rationale: Large-scale farmed-fish mortality at marine pens, reported by the state regulator's own data.

notes.harm: At least four million Atlantic salmon, 20,133 tonnes, died prematurely at Tasmanian farms in 2025 (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: The cited pieces report no closure or lost income; harvest was close to 68,000 tonnes of gutted salmon in 2024-25 (ref 1).
notes.scale: Losses were recorded across the Tasmanian industry, a state coastline, not a single farm (ref 1).
notes.duration: December 2025 mortality exceeded 40 tonnes a day, and the Macquarie Harbour 2023 to 2024 losses show repeat events across more than two years (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: The EPA publishes mortality data and the EPA had received 62 mortality reports since 1 August 2024 by January 2025, a formal reporting channel but not an enforcement order (ref 2).

records.title: Hauraki Gulf Marine Protection Act 2025 protects part of the Marine Park but leaves most bottom trawling in place
records.description: New Zealand's Hauraki Gulf / Tikapa Moana Marine Protection Act took effect in October 2025, extending two marine reserves, creating high protection areas and five seafloor protection areas where trawling, Danish seining and dredging are banned. Greenpeace and LegaSea say bottom trawling remains allowed across much of the Gulf, and the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries rejected the proposed trawl-corridor restrictions in May 2025. Commercial ring-net fishing is allowed in two of the high protection areas.

location.name: Hauraki Gulf Marine Park
location.detail: Auckland and Coromandel region, North Island, New Zealand; the Marine Park covers about 1.2 million hectares (ref 3).

records.layer_rationale: Fishing-method impacts on seabed habitat in a protected coastal park, with a new protection law partly addressing them.

notes.harm: Greenpeace says bottom trawling remains allowed across much of the Gulf and is a major driver of habitat damage; the harm is described, not measured, in the cited pieces (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: The five seafloor protection areas ban trawling, Danish seining and dredging, and ring-net fishing is allowed in two of the 12 high protection areas (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The issue concerns a single marine park of about 1.2 million hectares (ref 3).
notes.duration: The 2023 consultation proposed bans on up to 89% of the park, and the 2025 Act left most of that unadopted, so the issue spans 2023 to 2025 (refs 1, 3).
notes.significance: Parliament passed the Hauraki Gulf / Tikapa Moana Marine Protection Act in 2025 and the Minister rejected trawl corridors in May 2025 (ref 1).

records.title: Lord Howe Island coral bleaching in 2024 and continuing heat stress in 2025 at the world's southernmost reef
records.description: UNSW and University of Newcastle researchers found bleaching across every site they surveyed at Lord Howe Island in early 2024, with heat stress of 20 Degree Heating Weeks, the highest recorded for the region. A severe low tide in May 2024 then killed corals exposed above the waterline, and the reef was still under heat stress in 2025. The lead researcher said recovery for these southern subtropical reefs is extremely slow.

records.title: NSW shark nets: bycatch of non-target animals, a scientific review and stalled removal trial, 2025

The Newcastle Herald reported that 223 animals were caught in the 2024-25 season, only 24 of them target sharks, and 149 of the 199 non-target animals did not survive. A March 2025 review by the state's Threatened Species Scientific Committee found no evidence the program reduces shark-related fatalities, and a trial to remove nets from three beaches had stalled by September 2025.

records.title: Giant kelp forests on Tasmania's east coast down about 95%, with a restoration project under way
records.description: An estimated 95% of giant kelp forests on Tasmania's east coast have disappeared, with Nature Australia citing heatwaves, a strengthening East Australian Current, competing seaweeds and sea urchin overgrazing. A 3.5 million AUD Tasmanian Giant Kelp Restoration Project has run since 2024 at 18 coastal sites, and hundreds of giant kelps have reached the surface at several sites after being absent for a decade.

location.detail: East coast of Tasmania, Australia; the cited pages name no individual restoration sites.

records.layer_rationale: Loss of a canopy-forming habitat from warming and urchin overgrazing, with active restoration.

notes.harm: An estimated 95% of east coast giant kelp forests have disappeared (ref 1) and Nature Australia puts the decline at over 95% since the 1970s (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No lost fishery income is reported; the sources say a developing urchin fishery is used as a control method and supports regional jobs (ref 2).
notes.scale: The loss covers the east coast of Tasmania, a regional coastline (ref 1).
notes.duration: The decline is described as running since the 1970s, with sites absent of kelp for a decade (ref 2).
notes.significance: The cited pieces are a magazine report and a conservation group page; no formal listing or order is cited.

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: An estimated 95% of giant kelp forests on Tasmania's east coast have disappeared (Outback magazine, ref 1).

records.title: Star of the South offshore wind farm environmental statements open for comment, with whale protections debated
records.description: The proposed Star of the South wind farm, up to 147 turbines and 2.2 GW, 10 to 40 km off Gippsland in Bass Strait, put its draft Commonwealth EIS and Victorian EES out for public comment in 2026, with submissions closing on 29 June. The Dolphin Research Institute judged the whale and dolphin assessments thorough but improvable, recommended conditional approval and asked for observers and expanded humpback protections. VRFish told recreational fishers who use the area to review the documents.

notes.significance: A draft Commonwealth EIS and Victorian EES were released for public comment, a formal assessment step (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Otway Basin seismic survey proposals opposed over whale risk, with a 2026 regulator rejection of one plan
records.description: Seismic survey proposals in the Otway Basin off Victoria have drawn objections over harm to whales and fisheries. A TGS 3D survey of about 5.5 million hectares in the Australian Whale Sanctuary received more than 30,000 submissions and was abandoned in 2024, and in February 2026 the Environmental Defenders Office reported that the offshore regulator NOPSEMA rejected a CGG plan for not adequately addressing impacts on marine life.

records.layer_rationale: Offshore petroleum exploration noise assessed against whale recovery plans, with a regulator decision.

notes.harm: The regulator found the CGG plan could displace pygmy whales from foraging areas and was not consistent with blue and southern right whale plans; no harm was recorded because surveys did not proceed (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Fishers including a rock lobster fisher said a reef he fishes was seismic-blasted and his pots came up empty afterward, an account in the 2022 coverage of an earlier proposal (ref 3).
notes.scale: The proposals span about 5.5 million hectares of Commonwealth waters off Victoria (ref 2).
notes.duration: The disputes run from 2022 (TGS and Schlumberger) through 2023 to 2026 (CGG), several successive proposals (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.significance: NOPSEMA rejected the CGG environment plan, per the Environmental Defenders Office (ref 1).

records.title: Orange roughy catch limit cut 57% for the Tasman Sea stock in 2024 with recovery in doubt
records.description: In September 2024 the Minister for Oceans and Fisheries cut the total catch limit for the Tasman Sea orange roughy stock (ORH 7A) by 1,221 tonnes, a 57% reduction. The Deep Sea Conservation Coalition said modelling showed the stock was already below an internationally agreed level and that none of four options would allow recovery within five years; Greenpeace and the Coalition want seamount bottom trawling halted.

notes.livelihoods: The total catch limit was cut by 1,221 tonnes, a 57% reduction, before the 1 October 2024 fishing year (ref 1).
notes.scale: The decision covers a single stock management area in the Tasman Sea (ref 1).
notes.duration: The stock assessment relies on 2013 survey data and later surveys in 2018 and 2023 point to continuing decline (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Minister made a formal catch-limit decision, and SPRFMO measures set a 40% biomass target over five years (ref 1).

records.title: Ex-Typhoon Halong storm surge floods Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta villages, setting a record at Kipnuk and Kwigillingok
records.description: On 12 October 2025 the remnants of Typhoon Halong drove a Bering Sea storm surge and winds of more than 50 mph onto the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta in western Alaska. The state counted 208 homes destroyed and 471 with major damage, about 1,600 people were displaced, and nearly all residents of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok were evacuated. The National Weather Service put the surge at Kipnuk at 6.6 feet above the normal highest tide, above the 4.7-foot record set in 2000.

location.name: Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta coast
location.detail: Southwest Alaska, United States: Kipnuk and Kwigillingok hardest hit; 49 to 52 communities reported damage

records.layer_rationale: Storm surge on a very low-lying coast, with the University of Alaska noting the delta lies within about 1.6 feet of the high tide line.

notes.harm: The state surveyed 3,472 homes and found 208 totally destroyed and 471 with major damage, with one confirmed death and two people missing in October reports (refs 2, 4).
notes.livelihoods: About 1,600 people were displaced, nearly all of Kipnuk and Kwigillingok were evacuated by air, and stored subsistence food was lost (refs 1, 4, 6).
notes.scale: The University of Alaska counted 49 communities with damage across the Y-K Delta and Norton Sound coasts, a regional stretch of the Bering Sea coast, not a single bay (ref 1).
notes.duration: Residents were still waiting to return in July 2026, nine months after the storm, and the region had flooded in summer 2024 as well (refs 9, 3).
notes.significance: The governor declared a state disaster on 9 October 2025 and the University of Alaska fact sheet records a federal disaster declaration approved on 23 October (ref 1).

population_affected.note: Estimated number displaced, from the University of Alaska fact sheet (ref 1); other reports use 1,000 to 1,800 depending on date.

records.title: Kipnuk and Kwigillingok vote to relocate to higher ground after Halong, but no federal route funds a move
records.description: After the October 2025 Halong flooding, more than 92 percent of the Kipnuk tribal members reached by phone voted to relocate about 13 miles northwest to ground 40 to 150 feet above sea level, while Kipnuk sits just over 10 feet above it. Kwigillingok also voted to move. The state plans to rebuild in place to pre-disaster condition and says recovery funds cannot pay for whole-community relocation.

notes.harm: The state put Kipnuk at about 90 percent destroyed and Kwigillingok at about 35 percent destroyed (ref 4), with two residents found dead and one never found by July 2026 (ref 4).
notes.livelihoods: Nearly all of the roughly 974 people who lived in Kipnuk remain displaced in Anchorage, Bethel and elsewhere, which is displacement of a community (ref 1).
notes.scale: Two villages with a combined population of about 1,000 are affected (ref 3).
notes.duration: Residents had been displaced for nine months by July 2026 and Kipnuk faced a second federal declaration after August 2024 flooding (refs 4, 5).
notes.significance: FEMA approved tribal disaster declaration No. 4912 for Kipnuk on 29 May 2026 and the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs held field hearings on 5 and 6 May 2026 (refs 5, 3).

records.title: Newtok abandoned to erosion as the last residents move to Mertarvik, with the Ninglick River cutting about 70 feet a year
records.description: Newtok on the Ninglick River lost about six homes and half its school to erosion and thawing permafrost, and the village council voted in August 2024 to shut down all critical infrastructure after the last residents chose to leave. About 230 residents had moved to Mertarvik from 2019 and the last 71 followed in 2024, but a June 2025 report found housing shortages and strained utilities at the new site. The move has cost about $160 million.

records.layer_rationale: River-bank and coastal erosion plus permafrost thaw forced a whole village to leave a low-lying shoreline.

notes.harm: Erosion and permafrost loss demolished roughly six homes and half of the public school at Newtok (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: Nearly 400 residents were moved about 9 miles to Mertarvik and Newtok's power and water plant were shut down, leaving the old village empty (refs 2, 3).
notes.scale: A single village site on one river bank, so the physical extent is local (ref 1).
notes.duration: Relocation has been underway for more than 30 years, with the last residents leaving in fall 2024 and the move still unfinished in June 2025 (refs 2, 3).
notes.significance: The village council voted unanimously in 2024 to shut down critical infrastructure, and Newtok was among six communities a GAO report deemed imminently threatened (refs 2, 1).

records.title: Four years after Typhoon Merbok, Norton Sound recovery money is still years away and Shaktoolik's $290 million move faces a funding gap
records.description: A September 2026 report says nearly $38.5 million in federal block-grant disaster recovery for Typhoon Merbok (2022) will take years to reach 53 eligible Western Alaska communities, with $5 million set aside for flood and erosion mitigation. Shaktoolik, on a gravel spit where Merbok washed away the protective cobble berm, has a relocation estimate of about $290 million, and a new storm surge of 3 to 5 feet was forecast for the southern Seward Peninsula in October 2026.

notes.livelihoods: Subsistence camps lost in the storm: the Kawerak relief fund took 147 applications worth about $2.5 million and has paid just over a quarter (ref 1).

records.title: Aleutian waters stay among the warmest on record after the Bering Sea heatwave years
records.description: NOAA's ecosystem status reports found Aleutian winter sea surface temperatures in 2022-23 were the warmest since 1900 and those of 2023-24 were among the ten warmest, while the eastern Bering Sea cooled to average conditions after record warmth in 2014 to 2021. NOAA reports poor groundfish condition in the Aleutians since 2012 and that Pacific cod eggs hatch only within a 3 to 6 degree range, which has been exceeded. NOAA did not update the eastern Bering Sea and Aleutian reports in 2025.

notes.harm: Aleutian Pacific cod, northern rockfish and Pacific ocean perch have had below-average condition since 2012 and cod eggs hatch only in a 3 to 6 degree range that has been exceeded (refs 2, 3).
notes.livelihoods: Several Bering Sea crab stocks kept declining, forcing disruptive harvest closures (ref 3).
notes.scale: Conditions span the whole Aleutian chain of about 1,100 miles and the eastern Bering Sea shelf (ref 3).
notes.duration: Aleutian winters were record-warm in 2022-23 and still among the ten warmest in 2023-24, after eastern Bering Sea heatwave conditions in 2014 to 2021 (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: NOAA Fisheries issues these formal annual ecosystem status reports to the North Pacific fishery managers (refs 1, 2, 4).

records.title: Ocean acidification linked to Bristol Bay red king crab decline in a 2025 NOAA study
records.description: A study led by Mike Litzow at NOAA's Kodiak Lab found that rising acidity explained about 21 percent of the Bristol Bay red king crab's variability in 1980 to 2023 and about 45 percent since 2000, while warming had little effect. NOAA's Ocean Acidification Program says acidification may be partly responsible for the 2021-22 and 2022-23 fishery closures. The authors stress that the result is a correlation, not proven causation.

location.name: Bristol Bay red king crab
location.detail: Bristol Bay and the southeastern Bering Sea shelf, Alaska, United States

records.layer_rationale: Falling pH in the cold Bering Sea is the physical driver tied to crab recruitment.

notes.harm: The study ties acidification to about 21 percent of red king crab recruitment variability over 1980 to 2023, a correlation rather than proven causation (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: NOAA says acidification may partly explain the 2021-22 and 2022-23 Bristol Bay red king crab fishery closures (ref 3).
notes.scale: Ocean models show pH across the Bering Sea approaching thresholds that reduce juvenile survival (ref 1).
notes.duration: The signal spans 1980 to 2023 and strengthens since 2000, at 45 percent (ref 2).
notes.significance: A peer-reviewed study and NOAA's Ocean Acidification Program statement, with a NOAA acidification indicator now in the annual ecosystem status report (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: No population figure in the cited sources.

key_measure.text: Acidification explained about 21% of the red king crab decline over 1980 to 2023 and about 45% since 2000 (ref 1); the OA-ICC summary words this as recruitment variability (ref 2).

measures.note: AOAN says 'population decline'; OA-ICC says 'recruitment variability' (refs 1, 2).

measures.note: Same study (refs 1, 2).

signals: Bristol Bay red king crab fishery closures in 2021-22 and 2022-23 (ref 3).

trend.note: The acidification share rises from 21% (1980 to 2023) to 45% (since 2000) (ref 1).

records.title: Paralytic shellfish toxins in Aleutian mussels hit 47 times the legal limit in 2023
records.description: NOAA's 2023 report found paralytic shellfish toxins in blue mussels from Sand Point, Unalaska, False Point and Akutan in June 2023 at 47 times the legal limit. A year later Unalaska mussels were still seven times the limit, and NOAA's 2024 Bering Sea report card said harmful algal blooms are becoming more prevalent in the northern Bering Sea. The 2022 report had recorded 3.4 times the limit.

records.layer_rationale: A harmful algal bloom toxin in shellfish is a marine bloom pollution problem rather than a land nutrient load.

notes.harm: Blue mussel toxin levels were 47 times the legal limit in June 2023 and 7 times at Unalaska in 2024 (refs 1, 2).
notes.livelihoods: The cited NOAA pages report the exceedance but describe no closure or advisory, so no restriction is documented here (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: Four communities across the eastern Aleutians and Alaska Peninsula were sampled, a stretch of coast, not a single bay (ref 1).
notes.duration: Exceedances recurred in 2022 (3.4 times), 2023 (47 times) and 2024 (7 times) (refs 4, 1, 2).
notes.significance: NOAA's formal annual ecosystem status reports flag the exceedances against the legal limit (refs 1, 2).

population_affected.note: No count of people affected in the cited sources.

records.title: Fuel and hazardous-material spills from Halong flooding hit Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta villages
records.description: Flooding from ex-Typhoon Halong damaged bulk fuel storage in western Alaska villages, with fuel drums floating through Nightmute and a sheen on the water. The Coast Guard reported a light sheen on 13 October 2025 and the state later reported a hazardous materials spill at Nightmute with a boil-water notice for traditional outdoor water sources. A February 2026 report lists heating oil, diesel and sewage among the substances released.

records.title: Bering Strait traffic nearly doubled to 665 transits in 2024, raising oil spill risk on both sides
records.description: The Oil Spill Recovery Institute reports that 665 vessels transited the Bering Strait in 2024, 362 on the Russian side and 303 on the U.S. side, close to double the traffic of 15 years earlier. Russian traffic is dominated by tankers and large cargo vessels carrying fuel or crude oil, and substandard or low ice class ships are using the strait to enter the Northern Sea Route. In June 2025 the Coast Guard's Arctic Coordinator helped lead a Nome drill for a simulated 150,000 gallon diesel spill.

notes.harm: No spill is documented; the risk is potential harm, with a marine biologist warning that heavier bunker fuel could affect marine mammals, seabirds, fish and crab (ref 2).
notes.livelihoods: No route or fishery restriction is reported in the cited sources (refs 1, 2).
notes.scale: The strait is shared by the U.S. and Russia and a Russian-side spill could reach U.S. waters (ref 1).
notes.duration: Transits have nearly doubled over 15 years, a chronic rise (ref 1).
notes.significance: The Oil Spill Recovery Institute issued a formal request for proposals for an updated risk analysis, with applications due 16 January 2026 (ref 1).

records.title: Bering Sea snow crab fishery rebuilds slowly after the heatwave collapse, with the 2026-27 quota cut about 45%
records.description: NOAA scientists report that more than 10 billion snow crab disappeared from the eastern Bering Sea after 2018, and the fishery was closed for two consecutive seasons from October 2022. It reopened in 2024-25 at 4.72 million pounds, rose to 9.3 million pounds in 2025-26, and Alaska announced 5.1 million pounds for 2026-27. A December 2025 NOAA study attributes the collapse to warm water and crowding that limited the crabs' energy reserves, and calls recovery fragile.

location.detail: Bering Sea District west of 165 W longitude, fished out of Dutch Harbor and St. Paul, Alaska, US

records.layer_rationale: A commercially fished crab stock collapsed after a marine heatwave and is rebuilding under reduced quotas.

notes.harm: The Science paper reports that the eastern Bering Sea lost more than 10 billion snow crab after 2018 and that the population hit historic lows in 2021 (ref 4).
notes.livelihoods: The fishery was shut down in October 2022 and stayed closed for two seasons, a loss of the fishery for that period, and a $123.6 million federal fishery disaster allocation was reported in 2026 (refs 3, 5).
notes.scale: The finding concerns one stock, the eastern Bering Sea snow crab, even though it spans a large part of the shelf (ref 1).
notes.duration: The decline began in 2018 and quotas in 2026-27 remain far below the 45 million pounds of 2020-21, so the effect has lasted more than eight years (ref 3).
notes.significance: State and federal managers closed the fishery for two seasons, and the Commerce Department allocated disaster funding for the fishery (refs 3, 5).

population_affected.note: The sources describe crab and fleet effects, not a count of people.

key_measure.text: The 2026-27 Bering Sea snow crab total allowable catch is 5.1 million pounds, about 45% below 2025-26 and far below 45 million pounds in 2020-21 (ref 3).

records.title: Bristol Bay red king crab reopens at small quotas after the 2021 closure, with young crab scarce for about 15 years
records.description: The Bristol Bay red king crab fishery had been closed since 2021, its first closure in roughly 25 years, when KUCB reported in October 2023 that male and female crab were at historic lows and recruitment had been very low for about 15 years. ADF&G has since announced quotas of 2.31 million pounds for 2024-25, 2.68 million for 2025-26 and 3.41 million for 2026-27, each after survey biomass exceeded the opening thresholds.

notes.livelihoods: Quotas of 2.31, 2.68 and 3.41 million pounds in 2024-25 to 2026-27 are small restrictions on a fishery that was closed in 2021-2023 (refs 2, 3, 4).
notes.scale: The finding covers a single stock, the Bristol Bay (Area T) red king crab (ref 3).
notes.duration: KUCB reports weak recruitment for about 15 years and a closure that began in 2021, and quotas are still small in 2026 (refs 1, 4).
notes.significance: ADF&G and NMFS issued formal annual total-allowable-catch advisories after survey thresholds were met (refs 2, 3).

records.title: Council recommends a 45,000-fish Western Alaska chum bycatch limit for the Bering Sea pollock fleet
records.description: In February 2026 the North Pacific Fishery Management Council recommended a limit of 45,000 Western Alaska chum salmon for the Bering Sea pollock fishery, with a corridor closure if a sector reaches its share. The recommendation goes to the Secretary of Commerce and National Marine Fisheries Service before it can take effect. Tribal groups link repeated Yukon and Kuskokwim closures to weak chum runs, while industry groups say hard caps risk early fishery shutdowns.

location.name: Bering Sea pollock grounds north of Unimak Pass
location.detail: Southeastern Bering Sea shelf, Alaska, US; salmon bound for the Yukon, Kuskokwim and other Western Alaska rivers

records.layer_rationale: Incidental catch of salmon in the pollock trawl fishery affects Western Alaska salmon stocks and the communities that depend on them.

notes.harm: The council says about 17% of chum caught over the past decade were bound for Western Alaska rivers and that declines across the North Pacific appear driven largely by warm water, so bycatch harm is partial (refs 1, 5, 6).
notes.livelihoods: Tanana Chiefs Conference testified that closures over six years cost its region about $27 million in direct income, and a Kuskokwim commission official said there is no more commercial fishing income (ref 1).
notes.scale: The issue spans the southeastern Bering Sea pollock grounds and the Western Alaska river systems the salmon return to (refs 2, 3).
notes.duration: Dozens of Yukon communities were in their sixth year of near-total salmon fishing closures in June 2025, and chum bycatch peaked above 500,000 fish in 2021 (ref 5).
notes.significance: The council made a formal recommendation to the Secretary of Commerce in February 2026, but it is not yet a federal rule (refs 2, 3).

population_affected.note: The sources describe Yukon and Kuskokwim communities generally without a population figure.

key_measure.text: The council recommended a bycatch limit of 45,000 Western Alaska chum salmon for the Bering Sea pollock fishery, with a corridor closure and sector apportionments (ref 3).

records.title: Court challenges to EPA's 2023 Pebble mine veto await a ruling after June 2026 hearing
records.description: EPA issued a Clean Water Act section 404(c) Final Determination on 30 January 2023 that limits disposal of dredged and fill material for the proposed Pebble deposit in waters important to Bristol Bay salmon. Pebble Limited Partnership, the State of Alaska and two Alaska Native village corporations challenge it in federal court in Anchorage, where Judge Sharon Gleason heard about 150 minutes of argument on 25 June 2026. The Justice Department and Bristol Bay intervenors defend the veto, and no ruling had been reported in the cited articles.

notes.significance: EPA's 404(c) Final Determination is in force and a federal district court heard oral arguments on 25 June 2026 with a decision pending (refs 1, 2).

records.title: Northern fur seal pup production keeps falling on St. Paul Island as a 2026 lawsuit targets pollock trawl catch limits
records.description: NOAA's Alaska stock assessment (revised July 2025) reports that St. Paul Island pup production declined 3.95% a year from 1998 to 2022 and that the Eastern Pacific stock remains depleted under the Marine Mammal Protection Act, with the cause of decline unknown. On 8 April 2026 the Center for Biological Diversity sued NOAA Fisheries in federal court in Alaska, alleging that pollock trawl catch limits cause prey competition for seals. NOAA Fisheries has said there is not sufficient information to determine whether the fishery disrupts St. Paul seals.

records.title: Northern Bering Sea Climate Resilience Area leasing withdrawal has been revoked, reinstated and extended across three administrations
records.description: Executive Order 13754 created the Northern Bering Sea Climate Resilience Area in December 2016 and closed parts of the northern Bering Sea and Norton Sound to oil and gas leasing. A 2017 executive order revoked it, and Executive Order 13990 reinstated it in 2021. records.title: Vaquita survives in the Upper Gulf of California: 2025 cruise reports 7 to 10 animals and new calves while gillnets remain in the wider refuge
records.description: Mexico's environment ministry reported sightings of between seven and 10 vaquita porpoises and the birth of new calves during the May to September 2025 observation cruise, and the conservation commission said monitoring showed no substantial decrease over three consecutive years. The IUCN Cetacean Specialist Group report on the joint visual and acoustic survey says gillnets have been nearly eliminated from the sanctuary since 2022 but the wider Vaquita Refuge remains heavily fished, and an unprotected area of high vaquita use lies northwest of the sanctuary extension.

records.title: Coral bleaching across Eastern Tropical Pacific reefs from April 2023: 38 of 72 monitored sites severely bleached

records.title: Marine heatwaves on Chile's coast and Northern Humboldt build into an El Niño in 2025-2026
records.description: The SPRFMO 2025-2026 ecosystem status report counts six marine heatwaves totalling 179 days off northern Chile, including a 109-day event in early 2026, with the first events already in late 2025. records.title: Central Chile's urban beaches erode faster as swells intensify, with Reñaca and Santo Domingo among the worst
records.description: A Universidad Católica study by the Observatorio de la Costa tracked 66 beaches between Arica and Chiloé and found retreat accelerating between 2023 and 2024, with Santo Domingo at 5.7 m a year and Hornitos at 5.2 m a year. In September 2026 T13 reported swell damage on Valparaíso-region beaches including a sand cliff on Reñaca beach, damaged walkways at Acapulco and gravel replacing sand at La Boca. Researchers cite more frequent storm swells since 2015, sediment deficit and building on dunes and wetlands.

records.title: Petroperú crude spill from the Talara refinery terminal oils beaches and reaches the Grau marine reserve
records.description: Petroperú reported a crude spill on 20 December 2024 during pre-loading manoeuvres at the Talara refinery's multi-buoy terminal. OEFA measured 47.14 hectares of intertidal and 228.74 hectares of subtidal area affected from the refinery to Cabo Blanco, and the environment ministry declared a 90-day environmental emergency. Olive ridley turtle hatchlings were among wildlife affected.
