records.title: Mass intoxications of schoolchildren around Quintero Bay in 2025 leave the cause unidentified
records.description: From late September 2025, odours of gas and chlorine around Quintero Bay coincided with hydrocarbon loading operations and sent 127 students and teachers, then nearly 200 people, to health centres, with over 100 diagnosed with T59 toxic-gas intoxication. AIDA and Greenpeace filed a protection action on 8 November 2025 in Valparaíso asking for automatic industrial shutdowns and full compliance with the 2019 Supreme Court ruling. The cause had not been identified in the sources opened.

location.name: Quintero Bay and Puchuncaví
location.detail: Quintero and Puchuncaví communes, Valparaíso region, around the Quintero Bay industrial and port complex that also includes Concón.

records.layer_rationale: Toxic-gas exposure episodes tied to an industrial and hydrocarbon port complex on the bay.

notes.harm: More than 100 of nearly 200 people attending health centres were diagnosed with T59 intoxication, mostly minors, across nine schools (refs 3, 4).
notes.livelihoods: A health alert was in force in the Concón, Quintero and Puchuncaví industrial belt and schools were affected, an advisory rather than a closure of fishing or ports (ref 1).
notes.scale: The episodes centre on two communes and one bay, a local site (refs 3, 4).
notes.duration: Episodes in 2018, 2022, 2023 and again from September 2025 show recurring exposure over years (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: A 2019 Supreme Court ruling ordered preventive and corrective measures that the November 2025 protection action says are unmet, and an Inter-American Commission petition (P-1800-25) was sent to Chile in February 2026 (refs 4, 5).

population_affected.note: Almost 200 people attended health centres between late September and mid-November 2025, mostly minors (refs 3, 4).

records.title: Chile extends its red tide health alert for Los Lagos and Aysén to April 2027
records.description: Chile's health ministry extended by decree 50 of 7 April 2026, published 30 April, the red tide health alert for Los Lagos and Aysén to 30 April 2027, the latest renewal since the alert began in April 2022. The decree recalls paralytic shellfish poison at 14,018 µg per 100 g in Aysén against an 80 µg limit, a fatality, and six cases in Los Lagos including the death of a child under three. A thesis finds marine heatwaves can trigger Alexandrium catenella blooms when nutrients suffice.

location.name: Los Lagos and Aysén fjords and channels
location.detail: Shellfish-harvesting waters of Chile's Los Lagos and Aysén regions, including Estero Quiltralco in Aysén and Canal Quihua in Los Lagos named in the decree; a red tide was also found in Tongoy Bay, Coquimbo, in summer 2026.

records.layer_rationale: Harmful algal blooms that contaminate shellfish with toxins, fed by warm, calm, nutrient-rich water.

notes.harm: The decree records paralytic poison at 14,018 µg/100 g against the 80 µg limit at Estero Quiltralco, one death there and six cases in Los Lagos with a child's death (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Semanario Local describes sanitary closures halting extraction of clams, mussels, razor clams and other filter feeders, hurting fishing, aquaculture and tourism (ref 2).
notes.scale: The alert covers two regions of southern Chile, and a 2026 bloom also appeared in Tongoy Bay, a regional footprint (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: The alert began on 6 April 2022 and has been extended seven times, now to 30 April 2027 (ref 1).
notes.significance: Decree 50 of 7 April 2026 is a ministerial health-alert order with extraordinary powers, an enforcement-level instrument (ref 1).

population_affected.note: Six poisoning cases in Los Lagos in April 2022 cited in the decree, one fatal; a further death is recorded in Aysén in March 2022 (ref 1). No 2025-2026 case count was opened.

key_measure.text: Paralytic shellfish poison reached 14,018 µg per 100 g in Estero Quiltralco, Aysén, against a limit of 80 µg per 100 g (ref 1).

records.title: Mejillones Bay, a Chilean 'sacrifice zone', carries heavy metals and coal-port spills with fishers in decline
records.description: An AFP report of February 2024 says a 2019 regional study found significant heavy metals and organic matter in Mejillones Bay, linked to industrial waste and wastewater, and that about half of some 300 local fishers have left. A 2020 coal spill of about six tonnes at a port terminal came with more than ten similar spills in two years, and a 2019 Environment Ministry study found anoxic conditions. Chile plans to close the eight Mejillones coal plants before 2040.

notes.duration: Spills and contamination are described across 2018 to 2020 and still in 2024, a chronic condition (refs 1, 2, 3).

records.description: The Científicos de la Basura survey run with Universidad Católica del Norte sampled 179 beaches in ten Latin American countries in 2024 and found Peru had the most polluted beaches, followed by northern Chile, with Antofagasta the worst in Chile. records.title: Peru ends its 2026 first anchoveta season at about a quarter of the lowest quota in a decade, citing warm anomalous waters and juvenile fish
records.description: Produce opened the north-centre first anchoveta season with a total permissible catch of 1,914,049 tonnes, the lowest first-season limit in a decade apart from 2023 according to Infobae. After IMARPE's Eureka LXXVIII survey on 15 to 18 August 2026 found juveniles made up 65% of fish by number amid anomalous warm conditions, Produce closed the season from 21 August; a later ministerial resolution says it reached about 24.61% of its limit and exempted shipowners from the usual catch obligation.

location.name: North-centre anchoveta fishery, Peru
location.detail: Peru's coast from the northern limit of its maritime domain to 16 degrees S, the north-centre anchoveta zone managed by Produce and IMARPE.

records.layer_rationale: The world's largest single-species fishery lost most of a season to warm conditions and a high juvenile share, a stock and catch-limit problem.

notes.harm: IMARPE's Eureka LXXVIII survey found juveniles were 65% of specimens by number and 48% by weight and that somatic condition and fat content were low (refs 3, 4).
notes.livelihoods: Produce closed the season from 21 August 2026 and the fleet reached only about 24.61% of its limit, per the technical report cited in the ministerial resolution (refs 3, 4).
notes.scale: The measure covers the whole north-centre coast of Peru, a national fishery zone (ref 1).
notes.duration: The 2023 first season was never held, the 2025 first season closed early at 81.92% of a 3 million tonne limit, and the 2026 season ended in August (refs 2, 5, 3).
notes.significance: Produce issued a ministerial resolution authorising the season, a closure order, and a one-time exemption resolution published 15 September 2026 (refs 1, 3, 4).

population_affected.note: No affected-population figure appears in the cited sources.

records.title: Several hundred Chinese-flag squid vessels fish at the edge of Peruvian, Chilean and Ecuadorian waters as the jumbo squid stock sits in the red zone
records.description: Mongabay reports that China's own figures put its distant-water squid fleet at 528 vessels around the Ecuadorian, Peruvian and Chilean EEZs in 2024, and that 2024 jumbo squid catches fell to about 601,500 tonnes with the stock in the red zone of the Kobe diagram in four analysed cases. Chilean outlets reported 117 Chinese vessels detected off Chile in 2025 against 8 in 2024, and in July 2026 the Chilean Navy called a stationary concentration of about 370 Chinese-origin vessels near its territorial sea unusual; in Peru, artisanal fishers struck over a cut in the 2025 jumbo squid quota to 42,000 tonnes.

location.name: High seas beside the Peru, Chile and Ecuador EEZs
location.detail: Jumbo flying squid (Dosidicus gigas) grounds on the high seas adjoining the South American EEZs; the fleet moves between Chile, Peru and Ecuador through the year.

records.layer_rationale: An unregulated high-seas fishery for a stock reported in the red zone, with effects on coastal artisanal fleets.
secondary_drivers: No catch limit on the high seas

notes.harm: Mongabay Latam reports the stock in the Kobe red zone in four analysed cases and a 52% fall in catches in 2024 (ref 1); no mass mortality is documented.
notes.livelihoods: Peru's Produce cut the 2025 artisanal jumbo squid quota to 42,000 tonnes by RM 00323-2025-PRODUCE and guilds said more than 5,000 artisanal boats were affected, prompting a strike in Piura (ref 5).

records.title: SPRFMO caps squid vessels at 651 and starts monitoring in 2027, but no catch limit is set and Peru's buffer-zone proposal is not approved
records.description: At its 14th meeting in Panama City on 2 to 6 March 2026 the SPRFMO Commission adopted a consolidated jumbo flying squid measure, electronic-monitoring standards and port-inspection amendments, and set a 2026 jack mackerel total allowable catch. According to Mongabay the vessel ceiling falls from 766 to 651, observer coverage starts at 5% of fishing days on 1 September 2027, the Scientific Committee again failed to agree a stock assessment, and Peru's proposed no-fishing buffer outside South American EEZs was not approved; Pew called the change insufficient.

records.title: Chile's common hake stays overexploited and its 2026 quota is cut again to about 29,000 tonnes, say Oceana and fishing unions
records.description: El Desconcierto reports that the Technical Scientific Committee for central-south demersal resources concluded at the end of 2025 that common hake (Merluccius gayi) still shows negative signals, with smaller fish and a rising share below the reference length, and recommended a 15% quota cut for 2026. Oceana Chile says the quota has fallen from 40,000 tonnes at the start of the current government to a maximum of 29,000 tonnes in a stock it describes as overexploited for twelve years, while Subpesca authorised an IFOP direct assessment survey in July 2026.

records.title: Chile's Law 21.752 reallocates catch shares between artisanal and industrial fleets in 20 fisheries through 2040
records.description: Law 21.752, signed on 19 June 2025 and published in the Diario Oficial on 25 June 2025, fixes a new artisanal-industrial split of catch quotas to 31 December 2040. For jumbo squid the artisanal share starts at 90% within a 90 to 80% range, for anchoveta and Spanish sardine in the north at 55% with a 55 to 85% range, and for common hake at 45% up to 35,020 tonnes, with excess quota going to the artisanal fraction up to a 50% cap.

notes.duration: Allocations are fixed until 31 December 2040 (ref 1).

records.title: Repeated algal blooms kill thousands of tonnes of farmed salmon in Los Lagos and Aysen, with a new Heterosigma bloom in Reloncavi Sound in 2026
records.description: Salmon farms in southern Chile lost about 1,500 tonnes in Reloncavi Sound in November 2023 and about 3,800 tonnes to a Pseudochattonella bloom in the Chonos Archipelago in January 2024, according to reporting on Sernapesca data. In April 2026 Sernapesca met producers after a Heterosigma akashiwo bloom affected 11 farm sites in Reloncavi Sound and authorised fish transfers and emergency harvests; its aquaculture deputy director said conditions anticipated a stronger El Nino.

location.name: Reloncavi Sound and Chonos Archipelago salmon farms
location.detail: Los Lagos region (Reloncavi Sound) and the Chonos Archipelago in Aysen, Chile's main salmon-farming regions.

records.layer_rationale: Recurring harmful algal blooms causing mass farmed-fish mortality and a disease aftermath.

notes.harm: About 3,800 tonnes of Atlantic and coho salmon were lost in the January 2024 Chonos bloom and about 1,500 tonnes in November 2023, per reporting on Sernapesca data (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Sernapesca authorised fish transfers, emergency harvests and longer holding periods at 11 affected sites in April 2026 (ref 2).
notes.scale: Events span two regions, Los Lagos and Aysen, rather than one farm (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Mass-mortality blooms are documented in November 2023, January 2024 and April 2026, a recurring pattern over about two and a half years (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Sernapesca coordinated contingency actions under an aquaculture pre-alert and the Navy and Subpesca joined an inter-institutional committee (ref 2).

records.title: Chilean salmon farms used 22.6% more antibiotics in early 2024; freshwater use fell 34% in 2025 while the national index rose
records.description: Sernapesca reported that salmon farms used 217.4 tonnes of antibiotic active ingredient in January to June 2024, up from 177.3 tonnes a year earlier, which it attributed mainly to piscirickettsiosis outbreaks after the late-2023 algal and low-oxygen events. For 2025, Sernapesca data show freshwater-phase use fell 34.1% but the national antimicrobial consumption index rose 5.88% on higher biomass, and the regulator targets a 25% cut over four years.

location.name: Chile's salmon farming regions
location.detail: Salmon farms in the Los Lagos, Aysen and Magallanes regions; 98.36% of first-half 2024 antibiotic use was in the seawater phase.

records.layer_rationale: Antibiotic use in marine net-pen farming releases active substances into coastal waters.

notes.harm: Sernapesca's figures show 217.4 tonnes of active ingredient used in half a year, mainly florfenicol, but the sources document no resistance or contamination measurement (refs 1, 3).
notes.livelihoods: No closure, restriction or income loss is tied to antibiotic use in the opened sources.
notes.scale: The data cover the national salmon industry across three regions (refs 1, 2).
notes.duration: Figures cover first-half 2024 and full-year 2025 freshwater use, a multi-year pattern (refs 1, 2).
notes.significance: Sernapesca issued a half-year report and a 25% four-year reduction target; Subpesca revised the sanitary programme in April 2026 (refs 1, 3).

records.title: Sernapesca logs 133 findings at salmon farms inside protected wild areas, while the Kawesqar reserve dispute over salmon concessions remains in the courts' record
records.description: Sernapesca's 2026 public account says a special programme carried out 926 inspections at 316 operating salmon farms in protected areas in 2025 and found 133 issues, within 258 regulatory breaches across 2,473 farms nationwide. In the Kawesqar National Reserve in Magallanes, the Third Environmental Court revoked two Nova Austral environmental approvals in January 2023 and said salmon farming appeared incompatible with the reserve's purposes without ruling on that question.

records.title: Peru's five-mile artisanal zone is contested as fishers protest a 2025 regulation and a congressional bill to allow mechanised purse seines
records.description: Supreme Decree 002-2025-PRODUCE, published in late February 2025, reserves Peru's first five nautical miles for artisanal and smaller-scale fishing and bans mechanised gear within three miles. Sechura fishers announced a strike for 10 March 2025 against it, while artisanal groups in Piura, Tumbes and Ancash demanded that Congress not pass a bill by five legislators allowing vessels of up to 10 cubic metres to use mechanised purse seines inside five miles.

location.name: Peru's first five nautical miles
location.detail: Peru's coastal strip of five nautical miles reserved for artisanal fishing, with protests in Sechura Bay (Piura), Tumbes and Chimbote (Ancash).

records.layer_rationale: A coastal access rule and a bill to weaken it set artisanal and mechanised fleets against each other.

notes.harm: Fishers argue that mechanised purse seines and trawls inside the first miles destroy ecosystems and favour illegal fishing, an allegation with no measured damage cited (ref 1).
notes.livelihoods: Sechura fishers say the decree would force them to seek permits or fish beyond three and five miles and strike on 10 March 2025 (ref 2).
notes.scale: The rule covers the national coastline and protests span Piura, Tumbes and Ancash (refs 1, 2, 3).
notes.duration: The documented dispute runs from late February to April 2025, a period of months (refs 2, 3, 1).
notes.significance: A supreme decree and a pending bill exist, and Congress voted 82 votes to return a committee report to the Production Commission (ref 1).
